name: West Coast Wilderness Trail
description: Rainforest, rivers and an easy roll beside the Tasman Sea.
text1:
The West Coast Wilderness Trail! One of many multi-day bikepacking trips you can find on New Zealand’s South Island. This trail is beautiful and does not require technical riding skills—or a suspension bike! The trail is 135 km long, with plenty of stops that make it ideal for a multi-day tour of the West Coast. Or, if you’re a strong rider, you could ride the whole thing in one go. Up to you!
This trail is a perfect connector between Greymouth and Hokitika. The coast road (State Highway 6) is a much less desirable option, with Westgold double-tanker dairy trucks carrying their high-quality product along the road at 100 km/h. It is not much fun having those things pass you while you’re cycling.
text2:
Travelling through the West Coast bush and taking in the countryside is far more peaceful and enjoyable. The section of State Highway 6 from Westport to Greymouth is more suitable for cycling. It still has traffic, but most large trucks head east via Lewis Pass (SH7) or Arthur’s Pass (SH73).
The trail starts by following the Tasman Sea. If the swell is right, you may find surfers and bodyboarders at the Blaketown breakwater. A short detour to the other side of the Grey River takes you to Cobden, which has a cleaner surf break, a surf club building at the tiphead, a mobile coffee cart and even a mobile sauna! The sauna opened in 2026.
After following the sea, the trail turns inland through lush native bush and farmland towards the town of Kumara, at around the 28 km mark. Greenstone Retreat is a great place to find accommodation, offering a villa, family rooms, campervan sites and tent sites. There is also the Theatre Royal Hotel.
Kumara is the last place to buy food before reaching Cowboy Paradise, near the trail’s highest point at 317 metres.
Note: Shantytown Heritage Park is not directly on the trail. Reaching it requires a detour of about 2 km from Paroa. It is a recreation of an old mining town, complete with a working steam train! If this tickles your fancy and you have time, it’s worth a visit.
text3:
From Kumara to Cowboy Paradise, the trail is often covered by a shady canopy—but you should still expect sun, rain and some of the best views of the entire ride! If you want to camp before reaching Cowboy Paradise, options are limited, but you may find an open patch of grass near Trapper’s Rest. Trapper’s Rest is not accommodation; it is an old gold-panning site marked on Google Maps.
Cowboy Paradise offers accommodation for cyclists, along with coffee and home-baked goods to refuel on. They accept only cash or bank transfers, so come prepared!
Just after Cowboy Paradise, the descent towards Hokitika begins, following the beautiful Arahura and Kaniere rivers. Lake Kaniere is an excellent place to stop for a swim, and there are also several holiday homes available to rent nearby.
If you feel like treating yourself to a glamping experience, Hurunui Jacks is the place to stay. It is right beside the trail and less than 20 km from Hokitika. Book in advance!
Hokitika is the pounamu capital of the West Coast. The town has several places where you can find the perfect piece or carving for a loved one. Hokitika is also home to the National Kiwi Centre if you’d like to see a kiwi.
There are plenty of places to eat. I recommend the Hokitika Sandwich Company, Dulcie’s Takeaways or a pie from Stone Oven Bakery. If you’re riding the trail in March, you might catch the Wildfoods Festival and find yourself eating huhu grubs, escargot, mountain oysters, locusts and snails—or trying some Fijian kava.
After Hokitika, the trail continues towards Ross. On the way, the West Coast Treetop Walk and zipline make for a fun detour. The Lake Mahinapua Hotel also has a pleasant patio where you can stop for a beer, as well as accommodation with hot tubs.
Most people travel the trail from north to south, but riding from south to north is just as enjoyable. Several local operators offer bike hire and shuttle services if you need transportation back to the start—or from the midpoint—of the trail.
The TranzAlpine train crosses the Southern Alps daily from Christchurch to Greymouth, creating a spectacular start to the journey, while scheduled flights connect Christchurch with Hokitika.
